issues.description: The problem statement (UML and task description) specifies addGuestStudents(int, String) — i.e., the method should accept a number of new guest students and a String reason — but the solution implements addGuestStudents(int) with only a single int parameter. This parameter mismatch will confuse students about the required method signature and cause tests or expected usages that rely on the reason parameter to fail.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the method signatures consistent. Either update the solution to implement addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, String reason) (and handle or record the reason appropriately, e.g., log or store it), or change the problem statement and UML to require only addGuestStudents(int). Preferably update the solution to match the specified UML signature and adjust implementation to use this.numberOfGuestStudents += numberOfNewGuestStudents.

issues.description: The problem statement (and UML) specifies a method addGuestStudents(int, String) — i.e., it expects two parameters (number of new guest students and a reason). The solution implementation provides addGuestStudents(int) with only a single int parameter. This mismatch between the expected method signature in the problem and the actual implementation in the solution creates a mapping/confusion for students: they may implement or call the method with two arguments (as required by the exercise) but the provided solution/template uses a different signature.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the implementation with the problem specification. Change the solution method signature to public void addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, String reason) and handle or document the reason parameter (e.g., store, log, or ignore it with a comment). Alternatively, if the reason parameter is intentionally unnecessary, update the problem statement/UML to require addGuestStudents(int) only — but prefer updating the solution to accept (int, String) to match the exercise.
